newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Brittan backs visa-free EU access for HK people.
newsitem.headline: Brittan backs visa-free EU access for HK people.

text.p: European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan spoke out on Monday in favour of granting Hong Kong people visa-free entry to Europe after the British colony reverts to China next year.

Brittan, in Hong Kong for a Europe/East Asia conference of the World Economic Forum, told government radio that letting Hong Kong people visit the European Union (EU) without visas was "reasonable" and in the interests of Europe.

Britain has agreed to allow visa-free entry for Hong Kong people after the handover to China next year, and Governor Chris Patten has been lobbying other nations to follow suit. But so far very few countries have responded positively.

"I think the governor's request is a reasonable one and one which will be not only in the interests of Hong Kong in the future but also in the interests of Europe and in the interests of the relationship between Europe and Hong Kong after next June," Brittan said.
"We strongly support that and are making our own representations with the member states of the European Union, but it is a matter that is in their hands and we can't dictate."
Up to 3.5 million of Hong Kong's 6.3 million people have travel documents issued by Britain and can travel extensively without visas under existing arrangements.

But most of the rest will have to travel with passports of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China, as it will be known after the handover next July 1. For them, visa-free travel is a big "if".
Brittan said relations between China and Europe were "much improved" and were now on a "realistic basis".

"We have made it quite clear that the continuation of present arrangements in Hong Kong and the observance of the agreements between Britain and China is a European interest and not just a British interest," said Brittan.

He said he hoped ties between the EU and Hong Kong would not change after 1997. It had been agreed with Lu Ping, China's Hong Kong policy boss, that Europe would continue to have a separate diplomatic representation in the territory, he said.
The European business community maintained "a huge interest in continuity", he said.
Brittan said he had raised questions of human rights during meetings with Chinese officials, adding that the moves had "not caused an explosion or anything of that kind".
He said there were limits to Europe's ability to police human rights in China.
"Europe can act as a watchdog. It can't act as a guarantor because it hasn't the capacity to do that," he said. "But Europe's concern for human rights is very real."
